turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I daresay, I am astonished that you would try to defend Wickham's character after the way you have treated him, and the way he has wronged others. You are not one to hesitate in speaking your mind, yet you seem reluctant to acknowledge your own role in his deceit. What is it about Wickham's misfortunes that you find so remarkable, I should like to know?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that your animosity towards me is quite...predictable. Given my actions towards your sister, I expected as much.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I must say, I am astonished that you still think yourself justified in your actions, despite the evidence of your own behavior. You speak of my animosity as if it were a personal failing, but I assure you, Mr. Darcy, it is merely a response to the harm you have caused.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist, Miss Bennet, that you are not in a position to lecture me on the nature of justification, considering your own family's...unseemly behavior.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You are still attempting to shift the blame, are you? First, you imply that I am lecturing you, when in fact I am simply pointing out the error of your judgment.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must say, Miss Bennet, your family's behavior is indeed a subject of great concern, and one that I have taken the liberty of observing for some time now. Your father's lack of prudence and your mother's foolish indulgence of their daughters' follies are hardly worthy of emulation. I daresay, you would do well to reflect on the influence you have grown up under.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am shocked that you would stoop to criticising my family, Mr. Darcy, when you have done nothing but perpetuate your own selfishness and pride throughout this entire conversation. Your attempt to lecture me on the influence of my upbringing is laughable, considering your own behavior towards my sister.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that I am not surprised by your continued refusal to acknowledge my good intentions and the sincerity of my feelings towards you. Your attachment to your own prejudices and misconceptions is as obstinate as ever, and I fear that we shall never come to a understanding.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your good intentions? You have shown me nothing but your own self-importance and a desire to control those around you. I will not be swayed by empty words, Mr. Darcy.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist that you do not misconstrue my actions, Miss Bennet. My behaviour towards your sister was merely a consequence of her own poor judgment and lack of propriety.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You have no right to lecture me on propriety, Mr. Darcy, when your own actions have been a constant affront to it. Your involvement in separating my sister from Mr. Wickham was a reprehensible display of your own self-interest and disregard for my family's well-being.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I suppose it is too much to hope that you will take responsibility for your actions and acknowledge the harm you have caused.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist that you do not continue to indulge in such gross exaggerations, Miss Bennet. My actions towards your sister were motivated by a desire to protect her from the influence of a man who has demonstrated himself to be utterly unworthy of her affections.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: How can you possibly justify your interference in my sister's life, Mr. Darcy? You have no right to dictate what is best for her or for anyone else.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that your persistent refusal to acknowledge my good intentions has grown tiresome. I shall not be lectured by one who has so little understanding of the complexities of the world.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am astonished that you still fail to see the harm your interference has caused, Mr. Darcy, and that you continue to justify it as a noble act of protection.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must suppose, Miss Bennet, that your own prejudices and biases against me have clouded your judgment, rendering you incapable of seeing the truth of my actions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am surprised, Mr. Darcy, that you can so easily absolve yourself of any wrongdoing, while attempting to cast aspersions on my character and judgment.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist, Miss Bennet, that you are being entirely unreasonable in your assessment of my character. Your lack of understanding and your propensity for misconstruing my actions are truly remarkable.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I must suppose, Mr. Darcy, that your own pride and obstinacy have led you to misjudge the situation entirely, and that you are now attempting to justify your own actions by casting aspersions on my character.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
